source.title: Feature Contamination: Neural Networks Learn Uncorrelated Features and Fail to Generalize
source.authors: Tian-Ren Zhang; Chu-Jie Zhao; Guanyu Chen; Yi-Zhou Jiang; Feng Chen

record.tranche_reason: The study presents theoretical, numerical, and empirical results for feature contamination and explicitly contrasts this mechanism with superposition, arguing that neural networks can learn uncorrelated features even when there are enough neurons to represent features separately. It does not test the original sparse-feature superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports representation-distillation and OOD-performance results, but those do not measure the listed versions. Its discussion of superposition is not itself a result; the rows below are based on its own feature-learning results.
record.test_reason: The paper's own theory and numerics show neuron weights in two-layer ReLU networks picking up label-uncorrelated background features alongside core features, with width m ≥ Θ(d0). So the neurons mix features without any capacity shortage. This bears on V3 (polysemantic-like mixing from a non-capacity cause, here activation asymmetry under SGD). It does not test the sparse toy-model geometry (V1), LLM or SAE evidence (V4, V5) or feature dimensionality (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusion is that SGD-trained nonlinear networks learn label-uncorrelated background features alongside core features (feature contamination), and that this drives OOD failure distinct from spurious correlations; linear networks provably avoid it. The contrast with superposition appears only in a related-work paragraph (Appendix G.3): networks learn uncorrelated features 'even when it has enough neurons'.
record.recipe_differences: Studies SGD feature learning and projections onto orthogonal core and background features, not sparse-feature superposition, its sparsity sweep, or its geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported contamination differs between ReLU and linear networks; the paper attributes the difference to nonlinear activation asymmetry.

fits_no_version.finding: Pre-trained CLIP-RN50 shows denser neuron activation than the distilled RN50 at similar ID accuracy; the authors read this as more 'decoupled' features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large-scale pre-training reduces nonlinear coupling of features in neurons (activation-density proxy, not a direct polysemanticity measure).

fits_no_version.finding: Class-conditional activation asymmetry and higher neuron selectivity after training in ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trained deep nets exhibit class-wise activation asymmetry, the proposed driver of feature contamination.

record.problems: Deep-network feature evidence includes qualitative visualizations. The paper notes that its setup leaves extensions to more general data distributions, multiclass classification, and more complicated architectures for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No other feature-projection results bearing on V2 or V3 were left out. Activation-asymmetry and OOD-risk results were not included because they do not directly measure the feature overlap named by these versions.

untested.parts: Not tested: more sparse features than dimensions, near-orthogonal overlapping directions, a sparsity-dependent transition, geometry. The features are orthogonal and dense, with m ≥ d0.
Not tested: competition for capacity, importance-based allocation of dedicated versus shared dimensions. The paper only argues that mixing occurs without capacity pressure (relevant to V3).
Not tested: LLM feature spread, SAE recovery.
Not tested: completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.
Not tested: prevalence of such mixed neurons in deployed or large models, and whether this contaminated mixing matches 'polysemanticity' as defined in the interpretability literature.

missing.what: Linear-network regression control: no background accumulation, small OOD risk
Generalization of feature contamination to GELU, Sigmoid and Tanh activations, trainable biases, AdamW, and nonlinear core-label relation (hyperball radii 1.0/2.0)
Main-text numerical feature-correlation curves (core and background both rise)

record.verdict_notes: Relation to superposition is indirect. 'Polysemanticity' here means neuron weight vectors projecting onto many orthogonal features, including label-uncorrelated ones, at width ≥ d0. I treat that as bearing on V3 only. V2 rows were unlinked because nothing tests capacity allocation; a reader might still read the result as narrowing V2 as a sole explanation. Rows are mostly figure-only or asymptotic statements with no numeric values.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test excess sparse features over dimensions, sparse co-activation, near-orthogonal overlapping directions, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular superposition geometry.

Does not measure feature importance or test whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while less important features share them. Tests whether neurons can accumulate predictive and uncorrelated background-feature components despite sufficient neuron capacity.

Does not establish the prevalence of polysemantic neurons in ordinary deployed models or test SAE-based identification. Tests feature contamination as an alternative mechanism in specified training setups.
No LLM feature-spread or SAE-recovery measurement.
Does not assess whether dictionary features are complete, stable, or canonical.
Does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features as units of superposition.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU neural network
rows.stage_stated: trained by SGD from random initialization
rows.operation_detail: Theorem 4.2 measures the learned weight projections onto core and background features after training.

conditions.value: orthogonal core and background features; background weights uncorrelated with labels

rows.measure: For Θ(m) neurons, the feature-weighted sum of core projections and the feature-weighted sum of background projections.
rows.value: Core sum = y · Θ(1); background sum = eΘ(1).
rows.locator: Theorem 4.2, Section 4; restated as Theorem B.2 in Appendix I
rows.note: The authors state that this occurs even when the network has enough neurons to represent all features separately. This is evidence for feature contamination, not a test of sparse superposition geometry.
rows.check: Link to V2 removed. The row measures mixing without capacity pressure, not whether capacity competition allocates dedicated dimensions by importance. That bears on V3. Value and state are correct.

relationships.condition: Two-layer ReLU networks trained by SGD with weight decay on orthogonal core/background features, m ≥ Θ(d0); classification (theory and numerics) and regression
relationships.reason: Neurons accumulate Θ̃(1) projections onto label-uncorrelated background features alongside core features despite ample width, i.e. mixing without capacity pressure (R1, R3, R5).
relationships.display_finding: Despite ample width, neurons accumulated Θ̃(1) projections onto label-uncorrelated background features alongside the core features, so features mixed without capacity pressure.

source_check.reason: R1 proves simultaneous core/background projections; R3 and R5 demonstrate contamination numerically with m=256 and 64 input features. Appendix G.3 explicitly states that sufficient neurons do not prevent learning uncorrelated features.

relationships.condition: Two-layer linear networks in the matched theoretical and classification settings
relationships.reason: With identity activations, background projections stay ≤Õ(1/√d) and do not accumulate. The non-capacity mechanism depends on nonlinearity (R2, R4).
relationships.display_finding: With identity activations, background projections stayed at most Õ(1/√d) and did not accumulate, so the mixing mechanism depends on nonlinearity.

relation.reason: Its own theoretical and numerical results demonstrate core/background mixing without capacity shortage, bearing on V3.

tranche.reason: The study demonstrates feature mixing with sufficient representational capacity and explicitly contrasts this with capacity-limited superposition in Appendix G.3, qualifying a capacity-only explanation.

source_check.notes: Evidence for V3 operationalizes mixing through feature-weight projections; equivalence to interpretability polysemanticity remains an inference. Figure 9(b) also supplies a linear regression control, outside the five listed rows; cross-study status counts were outside this study-only check.

statements.correction: Theorem 4.2 measures simultaneous core/background feature-weight projections. Appendix G.3 contrasts feature contamination with capacity-limited superposition. Correspondence to interpretability definitions of polysemanticity is not tested or explicitly discussed.
statements.problem: The paper does not explicitly leave correspondence to interpretability polysemanticity open; that is the synthesis's methodological inference.
